title: Millions of personal records in Japan, South Korea exposed amid surge in AI-powered cyberattacks
key_facts: A wave of cyberattacks in Japan and South Korea is leaking tens of millions of personal records; Masaaki Taira, who chairs the ruling Liberal Democratic Party's cybersecurity body, called it a 'national cyberspace emergency' on 9 Oct.
South Korean President Lee Jae Myung warned that AI lets amateur hackers breach systems without specialised skills.
Japan had over 600 corporate cyber incidents by early October 2026, more than in all of 2025.
On 7 Oct a ransomware attack on SoftBank subsidiary IDC Frontier disabled cloud services for 495 corporate and municipal clients; frozen-food distributor Nissui froze shipments to 1,200 partners.

Largest leaks include Sourcenext (22.51 million records), Skyticket (14.64 million), Burger King (11.18 million) and, on 16 Oct alone, Yamato (5.3 million) and Nikkei (1.83 million); 1.6 million driver's licence images from Park24's Times Car were reportedly sold on the dark web.

In South Korea at least 16 financial institutions, among them Shinhan Bank and KB Kookmin Bank, were hit in late September and early October, exposing about 100,000 customer contact and borrowing records; CrowdStrike tied them to a Chinese-speaking actor using an open-source AI-driven tool, ARTEX.

Experts told the paper the attacks are mainly financially motivated and that there is no evidence of direct state involvement; Harumichi Yuasa of Meiji University said incidents appear to involve advanced AI scanning for weaknesses.

New laws in both countries (Seoul's data-protection fines of up to 10 percent of revenue from 11 Sep; Tokyo's active cyber defence law from 1 Oct) appear inadequate against AI-driven attacks, the paper says.
quote_evidence: In Japan, over 600 corporate cyberincidents were reported by early October 2026, already surpassing the total recorded in all of 2025.

“While there is, at present, no evidence suggesting direct nation-state involvement, attackers are aggressively targeting entities holding vast stores of personal data to sell on underground markets for quick financial gain,” he added.
Cybersecurity experts told The Straits Times that the current spate of attacks is primarily financially motivated.
why_it_matters_hint: Customers face phishing and scams from leaked details, and shared vendors let one breach reach dozens of firms.
notes: Read in full at The Straits Times. The AI role is experts' reading ('appear to involve'), not a finding for each breach. Our 11 Oct 2026 edition carried the Financial Times on 20+ Japanese companies hit and our 14 Oct edition Japan Today on Japan seeking Anthropic's help.
